Some football streams online, but the sites are sketchy. For your football fix you will probably need to get an HD antenna and\or HD decoder box. I got a big one and instead of mounting it on the roof just stuffed it in my apt attic\crawlspace, its works just fine and picks up about 14 channels. That will give you your channel flipping fix, everything else like BBC and Scifi shows can be found on hulu\netflix or torrents.

This site will tell you what HD channels are available, https://www.tablotv.com/tools/ and this site will tell you what kind of antenna you need http://antennaweb.org/Address

If you really want to build your own collection and don't need too much live television, check out Plex; it's software that allows you to host your own video collection on your local LAN and steam it just like Netflix. You can load in your own DVDs and steam them without using the internet at all, which often provides better performance than online streaming. You also don't have to worry about your provider losing the rights to [X] show or not having [Y]. And the best part is, streaming has driven the price of DVDs down enough that it's much more affordable than a few years ago.

While I can't help with your specific wants (sifi, or syfy, or whatever the heck they've renamed themselves to this week) is the only blip on the radar, but since the end of Warehouse 13 and Eureka I'm not sure I've seen anything from them.

But onto the transition. We were a "TV is on anytime someone's home" type household. Out of bed and on with the news, then flip channels till we had to leave (or it was time for bed again). Not that we watched a lot, it was just channel skipping and "meh, this is good enough" watching. The first several months were hard to get past that routine, especially the news in the morning. I tried several of the free streams, but was using a HTPC and the ~3 minutes to get it up and running then spotty stream due to poor ISP connections meant not "watching" much. There's a lot more silence in the house now too, we don't just "leave it on" for background noise. When the silence gets a bit much, there are plenty of streaming music options (free and paid). I do this Much more frequently than my wife, but then again I work from home too.

Now we watch consciously, with intent. If something is playing, we're paying attention. If it's rubbish, we turn it off. Lots and LOTS of stuff we "used" to watch on pay-TV were culled very quickly once we started paying better attention.

We have tried the 3 majors (Prime, Netflix, Hulu), but only Netflix makes the cut when it comes time to put down the money. Hulu was flat out worthless, we weren't using it by the end of a 6 month trial and it was a no-brainer to cancel. Prime was sorta in the middle, some good stuff but Finding it was horrific (at least via their web page). Netflix wins, hands down, when it comes to variety and finding new stuff. I also go by the name Redbeard and wear a patch while my parrot perches on my peg-leg by using some unofficial add-ons for Kodi (used to be XBMC/Xbox Media Center).

As I said, I'm running a HTPC made out of an Intel NUC and control it via a network connection from my laptop. It's a geeky overkill setup, but I have zero limitations on what can be done and nearly unlimited control on what it looks like. We also have an old Roku, which is stupidly easy to operate and Roku always wins the awards when it comes to "which streaming device" because it's a 3rd-party operator, and absolutely anyone can use it with ease. If you're somewhat geeky and/or want to go the pirate route, you'll need something that can handle Kodi, which means an Android box (or small board computer, like the Raspberry Pi) at the minimum and a computer (laptop, desktop or dedicated HTPC) on the top end. I think I'd recommend the Amazon Fire BOX if you can live with their agenda (push their products heavily, possibly limit competitor streams, may turn over your data on a whim), else another android box or one of the small board computers.

You may be able to have access to some OTA TV stuff too (might cover some of the sportsball want). I'm way, Way outside the range of anything so I may be a little lacking, but check Antennaweb.org or tvfool.com ~ they will tell you what can be received OTA. Of course this could add complexity if you like/use DVR. You'll need a 3rd party DVR (or a computer to act as one), and if you want that signal to more than one TV/device (or on a tablet/phone/laptop), you'll need a device like the HDHomeRun.

Today I'm pretty much at the point where I'd be happy to simply not have a TV in the house at all. Wife doesn't agree, and she's got the final say in the matter. :)

Good luck. I certainly miss nothing for skipping out on paying for TV, the boob tube is on Far fewer hours of the day and we 'do' more things with the extra time.

I've been a cord-cutter for years. Here are my recommendations. Purchase a decent antenna. You can probably mount it on your old DirectTV "rod" after you remove the dish. You can probably re-use the wiring. Purchase a Roku as your starter device. This will give you access to the greatest quantity of streaming services including the big ones like Netflix, Amazon Prime, CBS News, Google Movies/TV, DishTV, Crackle, TubiTV, et.al. As someone else has mentioned, use Plex (free on Roku).

Explanation: As long as you live within reasonable distance from the broadcast towers, an antenna will help you get tons of free, HD, quality content. I get ~33 channels which gives me all the networks (ABC, NBC, CBS, PBS, Fox, CW) in high-def, as well as a ton of other channels.

Of all the streaming devices available, the Roku is the easiest to use and has the most content. Yes there are other good ones, but none has the content of Roku.

If you don't have Netflix and Amazon Prime, get them (both have a free 30 day trial). Netflix is only ~$10 a month and Prime is ~100 annually. Prime has tons of good perks, but we're getting it for the free streaming. Sign up for the free 1 month trial of SlingTV on Roku. This will give you ESPN, CNN, TNT, A&E, etc. It costs ~$20 monthly after the trial. If you don't watch it, cancel it. The other "must haves" for cordcutters are TubiTV, Crackle, and CBS News. These channels all have "free" content (with some commercials). TubiTV is my personal favorite--it might be a "private" channel on Roku, so if you go this direction, PM me and I will let you know how to add it. Crackle is a similar service run by Sony...not my personal favorite, but good content. CBS News is live 24/7 cable news, and I like it better than CNN/MSNBC/Fox News.

Plex is a very powerful app/channel/service and indispensable for cordcutters. Not only does it allow you to stream content (e.g. ripped videos) from your computer, you can also easily tell it to add online videos (e.g. YouTube videos) to your queue. Unlike other such services, Plex remembers where you left off (aka 'whispersync') so you can resume a local or online video right where you last left off.

There are a ton of other great services available, but the ones I've listed are the "must haves." I'm not a fan of Hulu, but I'd do the free trial IF SlingTV didn't meet your needs.

As an aside, I currently use Rokus, Chromecast, and an XBox One. Each have certain advantages, but the Roku is BY FAR the most versatile and content-rich device. It blows stuff like AppleTV away. So start there. They're cheap and a 75 year old woman could set one up.
